analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $7.25 an hour and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill, but the identical House companion became law in May 2007, raising the minimum wage to $7.25 an hour by 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 an hour over two years, and applied the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid introduced it as the first bill of the new Democratic Congress and it went onto the Senate calendar within days. The Senate never voted on S. 2 itself; instead the identical House bill (H.R. 2) carried the same wage increase into law, signed in May 2007 after Senate Republicans won a delay to add small-business tax breaks.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage, concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-paying service jobs, plus workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, who were previously outside federal wage law and would move up gradually from a lower island-specific rate to the federal wage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers, including in the islands

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps: to $5.85 within about two months of enactment, $6.55 one year later, and $7.25 two years later.
Applies the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, with a transition starting at $3.55 and rising $0.50 every six months until it reaches the federal rate.
The increase became law through the identical companion bill in May 2007, so millions of low-wage workers received the raise.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, and small businesses — through higher payroll costs, which can be passed to consumers as slightly higher prices; and businesses in the Northern Mariana Islands that had relied on the island's exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and small low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Employers who pay the minimum wage face higher labor costs on a schedule fixed in law, with no offsetting tax relief in this bill; the enacted version only added small-business tax breaks after Senate Republicans insisted on them.
Some economists argue that a higher wage floor can reduce hiring of the least-experienced workers, and low-margin businesses in places like the Northern Mariana Islands faced the steepest adjustment.
The Northern Mariana Islands' transition allowed a lower island wage for years, so island workers reached parity with the mainland slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The raise put more money directly in the pockets of some of the lowest-paid workers in the country, and the gradual three-step schedule gave employers time to adjust. The costs fall on low-wage employers and partly on consumers through prices, and the employment effects, while debated by economists, are generally small for increases of this size. On balance the trade was modest and well-targeted, though the bill offered no help to small businesses absorbing the higher payroll.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate put the bill on its calendar in the first week of January 2007 and never voted on it; the identical House bill carried the same wage increase through both chambers and became law in May 2007.

narrative.text: Harry Reid introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the first day of the new Congress, and it was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders on January 8 as Calendar No. 2.
The bill never received a Senate vote; the recorded action history ends with its placement on the calendar.
The identical House companion, H.R. 2, passed both chambers and was signed into law on May 25, 2007, enacting the same wage schedule and the Northern Mariana Islands provision.
Senate Republicans initially stalled the wage increase, demanding small-business tax cuts as the price of passage, which added roughly four months of delay before final enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage workers came out ahead: the raise they were promised became law through the House companion, so nothing was lost by S. 2 itself dying on the calendar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage workers, who got the raise anyway

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill as the first measure of the new Congress and moved it onto the Senate calendar within days.

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Was among the original senators who introduced the bill and had long pushed for the wage increase.

for.name: Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Was the only Republican cosponsor among the bill's 43 cosponsors.

for.name: George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the identical wage increase into law as part of the House companion bill in May 2007.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Initially blocked quick passage of the wage increase, insisting on small-business tax cuts as a condition, which delayed final enactment by several months.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 43 cosponsors included 40 Democrats, one Independent, and one Republican; the identical companion that became law passed the Senate 94-3 and the House 348-73.

industries.note: Restaurants employ a large share of federal minimum-wage workers, so the three-step raise directly raises their payroll costs. The burden can be passed to customers through menu prices.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Businesses that pay the minimum wage absorb higher payroll costs on a schedule fixed by the bill. The gradual phase-in limited the immediate hit.

industries.industry: Garment manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands
industries.note: The islands had been exempt from the federal minimum wage, letting garment factories pay far less while using Made-in-USA labels; the bill ended that exemption with a gradual transition.
